reason: The provided sources contain numerous cross-verified facts across independent sites supporting a compelling narrative about Uranus's extreme cold, axial tilt, discovery history, and magnetosphere.
story: In 1986, NASA's Voyager 2 swept past Uranus, giving humanity its first close-up view of the seventh planet from the Sun. Discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel—who initially mistook it for a comet—Uranus turned out to be one of the strangest worlds in the solar system. Even though Neptune is farther from the Sun, Uranus holds the record for the coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system, plunging down to a freezing minus 371 degrees Fahrenheit. Wrapped in methane gas that absorbs red light and gives the planet its signature blue-green color, Uranus spins almost completely on its side—likely the result of an ancient collision with an Earth-sized object. Taking 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun, Uranus's extreme tilt subjects its poles to decades of continuous sunlight and darkness. It also rotates backwards, features a lopsided magnetic field, and harbors moons named after Shakespearean characters.
angle: Despite not being the farthest planet from the Sun, Uranus has the coldest atmosphere in the solar system at minus 371°F.

claims.claim: Uranus has the lowest minimum atmospheric temperature of any planet in the solar system, reaching minus 371°F (49 K).
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.
Herschel initially reported his discovery of Uranus as a comet or star rather than a planet.
Herschel attempted to name the new planet Georgium Sidus after King George III.
Astronomer Johann Elert Bode suggested naming the planet Uranus after the ancient Greek sky deity.
Uranus has an extreme axial tilt of nearly 98 degrees, making it appear to spin sideways on its orbit.
Scientists theorize Uranus's severe axial tilt was caused by a long-ago collision with an Earth-sized object.
Uranus completes one orbit around the Sun every 84 Earth years.
Uranus's unusual tilt subjects its poles to prolonged periods of continuous sunlight followed by long periods of darkness.
Methane gas in Uranus's atmosphere absorbs red light, giving the planet its blue-green color.
Uranus rotates in a retrograde direction opposite to most planets, a characteristic shared only with Venus.
Uranus is the second least dense planet in the solar system after Saturn.
As of today, Voyager 2's 1986 flyby remains the only spacecraft visit to Uranus in history.
Uranus's magnetic axis is tilted roughly 60 degrees away from its axis of rotation.
The center of Uranus's magnetic field is offset from the geometric center of the planet by one-third of its radius.
Upper atmospheric winds on Uranus reach peak speeds of up to 560 miles per hour (900 km/h).
The moons of Uranus are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

disputed: Duration of seasonal darkness: S1 states each pole experiences 42 years of continuous darkness, while S3 describes a 21-year-long dark winter for half the planet. A script should state generally that the planet experiences decades of polar darkness without locking into conflicting exact figures.

Early discovery of Uranus's rings: S7 notes William Herschel claimed to observe a ring around Uranus in 1789, though mainstream astronomers dismissed it until the 1977 occultation discovery. A script should treat Herschel's ring observation as a disputed historical account ('according to one account').
